Summary

Three through stations under Paris

Every long-distance train to Paris ends in a dead-end station. This study tests replacing the four terminals used by high-speed trains by three deep through stations, joined by tunnels, so that high-speed, regional and suburban trains run across the city. It serves passengers better and nobody is further from a train than today; it would cost €55 billion to €70 billion; and on the benefits that can be counted so far it does not pay for itself.

€55 to 70bnto buildTwo layouts; €35 to 105bn across the range of prices
27.4 → 21.7minfrom a point in Paris to a station where the train stopsNo point is further than today. 26.1 min if the train's ride between its Paris stops is counted, the measure used for benefits
56% to 72%of running costs coveredWith €2.55 on each high-speed passenger. From 47% to 104% across the range of running costs
23% to 30%of the yearly cost returned in benefitsIf benefits stay flat. Comparable tunnels were approved with benefits between half and twice their cost

The findings

Passengers

Reaching a train gets quicker everywhere in Paris. Most trains stop at two stations, so the average time to a station where your train stops falls from 27.4 to 21.7 minutes. The stations stay where they are: no point loses.

Crossing Paris

5.2 million passengers a year stop changing stations by metro. A change that takes 57.5 minutes today becomes a direct train or a change of platform. Regional trains run on to a second station.

Cost

€70 billion with separate tunnels for high-speed trains, €55 billion without. Stations for 400 m trains are the largest item, at about €1 million per metre of platform track before add-ons.

Traffic

+2.6 million high-speed and +21 million regional journeys a year. Real, and small against the 107 million high-speed journeys that touch Paris today.

Financing

Running costs could be covered; construction cannot. A charge of €2.55 per departure or arrival brings €286 million a year; with other income that is 56% to 72% of running costs, but it loses more journeys than the project adds. Construction needs public money for its whole cost.

Economic return

Benefits counted: €0.86 billion a year, 23% to 30% of the yearly cost. Public budgets get back between nothing and a third of the repayment. The case depends on what is not counted yet: room for more trains.

The two accounts at a glance

What this means

As counted here, the project is a public investment paid by taxes and grants (€34 billion to €53 billion of grants on top of a new tax on businesses), with a return well below that of comparable tunnels. That is not yet a case for building, and not a case against studying: the count leaves out the reason most cities gave for through stations, capacity for more trains, and rests on prices and running costs taken from very few records. Five quick tests would confirm or stop the case.

How to use this document

The chapters follow the argument: the problem, what would be built, how it would run, what passengers gain, what it costs, who pays, what the country gets back, what could change the answer. Each can be read alone. Blue links with an arrow jump to the place where a point is treated; small numbers open the source.

Most figures can be explored: move a price in the cost chapter, a charge or a tax in the financing calculator, tap a point on the access map, pair two lines in crossing Paris, step through the works in the timeline.

Words used throughout. TGV: the French high-speed train. RER: the express suburban lines that already cross Paris underground. Layout A gives high-speed trains their own tunnels; layout B has them share with regional express trains.

Three annexes explain the precedents the project draws on: how Zürich turned a terminus into a through station under a working hall, what the Elizabeth line changed in London and how it was paid for, and how the Swiss timetable makes every train meet every train.

Every number comes from a small model described in method and assumptions, or from a document listed in the sources. Assumptions are marked assumption, drawings that are not designs illustrative sketch. No station has been designed; this is a first test of whether the idea is worth a study.

Chapter 1

Why Paris stops every train

Every long-distance line into Paris ends at a buffer stop, in one of four separate stations. So every train has to turn round, a passenger crossing France has to cross the city by metro, and the busiest stations are short of room for more trains. Other cities have removed the same problem by running trains through.

Four stations, four dead ends

4terminals for high-speed trainsGare du Nord, Gare de l'Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse. Inside Paris, no track joins one to another for long-distance trains
118platform tracks in the fourRER platforms included. Derived from published track lists, partly unverified1
5.2millionpassengers a year change station in ParisDerived from the last survey, in 2012-13, which counted 13,000 a day in the region2
57.5minfrom train to trainTaken in this study for a change of station today assumption The range assumed is 45 to 70 minutes

High-speed trains (TGV) from the north arrive at Gare du Nord, from the east at Gare de l'Est, from the southeast at Gare de Lyon and from the Atlantic coast at Montparnasse. Suburban and regional trains end at the same four stations.

All four are terminals: the track stops at the end of the platform, and a train can only leave the way it came. A through station is the opposite: trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back.

Three things follow from the dead ends. A train holds its platform for a long time while it turns round. A traveller whose trip continues beyond Paris has to change station. And each line reaches only one corner of the city. The rest of this chapter takes them in turn.

Words used in this report
  • TGV: the French high-speed train. A full train is 400 m long; two coupled sets carry more than 1,000 passengers.
  • RER: the five express lines, A to E, that already cross Paris underground. Suburban lines H, K, P, N and R do not: they end at the terminals.
  • Regional express: trains from towns 50 to 250 km away (TER and Intercités), which also end at the terminals.
  • Hall: the large room of a station where passengers wait before going to the platforms.

A terminal uses its platforms badly, and the big ones are short of room

A train that arrives at a terminal is emptied, checked, often cleaned and restocked, filled again, and sent back out across the tracks it came in on. At Montparnasse the nine tracks kept for high-speed trains give at most nine departures an hour: one train per track per hour.4 A TGV that only stops needs 3 minutes, or 4 to 5 at the largest hubs.5 Through stations are planned for four to six long-distance trains an hour on each platform track: that is the plan for Stuttgart's new station, which is not yet open.6 7 One that is in service, Zürich's Löwenstrasse station, handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks,8 though the through trains that wait for connections there stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).9 10

  • Gare du Nord was turned down as the terminal of the airport express for lack of capacity.13 It already handles 2,200 trains and 700,000 passengers a day.14
  • Gare de Lyon must find room. The high-speed line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030, and the station has to take them.15
  • The tracks cut the city. Approach tracks and platforms run from each terminal out to the ring road and divide the neighbourhoods on both sides. What the project would free is in changes to today's stations.

Crossing France means crossing Paris by metro

A traveller from Lille to Lyon gets off at Gare du Nord, takes the RER or the metro to Gare de Lyon and boards a second train. The last survey, in 2012-13, counted 13,000 passengers a day changing between two stations in the region.2 Scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since, that is about 5.2 million a year (derived; no newer count is published). With the stations joined, the same traveller stays on the train, or changes on the platforms of one station.

Two other groups of passengers pay for the dead ends.

  • Each traveller has one station to go to. A Parisian leaving for Bordeaux must reach Montparnasse, wherever in the city the trip starts. From the north-east of Paris that is a long metro ride with changes. Reaching the station measures it.
  • Suburban lines stop at the edge of the centre. Lines H, K, P, N and R each end at a terminal. A commuter from the northern suburbs who works in the south of Paris changes to the metro at Gare du Nord. Regional and suburban passengers gives the numbers.
Other cities have done it

Zürich put four through tracks under its terminal, Vienna replaced two terminals with one through station, and Stuttgart is replacing 16 terminal platforms with 8 through tracks.8 16 6 Paris itself did it for part of its suburban network with the RER. The annexes on Zürich and London give the record of two of them, and the next chapter describes what would be built in Paris.

Chapter 2

What would be built

Three deep stations under the existing ones, joined by 33.5 km of tunnel routes, with nothing left on the surface but the station halls. Every train stops at Paris Nord-Est. Trains from the southeast also stop at Gare de Lyon, and trains from the Atlantic at Montparnasse. Nothing here has been designed: the map and the quantities are planning assumptions.

Three stations and six tunnel corridors

3deep through stationsParis Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse: 52 platform tracks in layout A, 46 in layout B
33.5kmof route in six corridors100.5 km of two-track tunnel in layout A, 67.0 km in layout B
19.4kmof platform track400 m long for high-speed and regional express trains, 225 m for suburban trains
4station halls keptThe listed halls of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon, and the recent hall of Montparnasse, become the entrances to the stations below

A through station is a station where trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back. A corridor is a route followed by two or three tunnels side by side, each with two tracks. A portal is the place where a tunnel comes up to join an existing line. An underground junction is a cavern where two tunnels become one. The TGV is the French high-speed train. The RER is the set of express suburban lines that cross Paris underground.

The corridors run from each station to a point beyond the ring road, so that no surface track is needed inside Paris. Choose a layout, switch layers on and off, and select a station or a corridor to read its facts.

Two layouts: three pairs of tracks, or two

The same stations and corridors can be built in two ways. The report prices both.

Layout A: three separate networks

Each corridor has three pairs of tracks: one for suburban trains, one for regional express trains, one for high-speed trains. Nothing is shared. That is 100.5 km of two-track tunnel.

Layout B: two networks

Each corridor has two pairs: one for suburban trains, one for all main-line trains (high-speed and regional express together), as on the surface today. That is 67.0 km of tunnel. Main-line trains share platforms, which is assumed to save two tracks at each station assumption.

Cross-sections of one corridor, not to scale illustrative sketch. On the RER E extension opened in 2024, one tunnel 9.6 m wide inside carries two tracks.17

Chapter 3

How the stations would be laid out

Nobody has designed these stations. This chapter sketches where each would sit under the present station, what is already underground there, and how a passenger would get from the street down to the train. In the illustration used by the model, reaching a deep platform takes 4.0 minutes from the hall, against 3.7 minutes to walk down a terminal platform today. That near-equality rests on assumptions that a concept design must check.

Paris Nord-Est: one station under two halls

How to read the drawings

Every drawing in this chapter is an illustrative sketch. Only dimensions with a source, or taken from the model, are printed as numbers. Positions, shapes and the order of the platforms are invented to make the sketch readable. Dashed outlines mark structures whose depth is not published.

Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est are 500 m apart; the walk between them takes 8 to 14 minutes today.3 Between the two, about 30 m down, lies Magenta, a station opened in 1999 on line E of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground: 4 tracks in a cavern 225 m long and 54 m wide.19

The new station would be entered from either hall. In layout A it has 26 platform tracks, 24 in layout B. That is about 11 times the platform length of Magenta. Nothing of this size has been built under Paris.

What is not known. Whether 26 tracks fit on one level between the two halls, at what depth, and how they pass Magenta, the RER station of Gare du Nord and three metro lines. This station alone is carried at €16.0 billion in layout A with design, land and risk, 23% of the whole project. A concept design of it is the first study to commission; see what to verify.

Gare de Lyon: beside a five-level RER station, near the Seine

Gare de Lyon has 22 surface tracks in two halls (unverified);25 the seven platforms of Hall 1 are already 400 m long.26 Its underground station is one of the largest in Paris: RER lines A and D on five levels, 315 m long and 41 m wide, with RER D above RER A (unverified).27 The RER D tunnel is 20 m deep.28 Metro line 14 runs beside it (unverified).29

The new station would have 14 platform tracks in layout A and 12 in layout B. The natural place is under today's surface platforms, beside the RER station. That has not been studied.

Montparnasse: under a station already covered by a slab

Montparnasse has 28 platform tracks, 24 in the main station and 4 at its Vaugirard annexe.4 The platforms are one level above the street: Hall 1 is on level 2.31 They are already covered by a slab that carries a garden of 3.5 hectares, the Jardin Atlantique (unverified).32 Four metro lines meet around the station (unverified).33

The new station would have 12 platform tracks in layout A and 10 in layout B. This part of Paris stands over old limestone quarries: 770 hectares of the city are undermined, in eight arrondissements that include the 14th and 15th, where the station stands.34

How deep, and why

The new platforms have to pass under what is already there: metro lines, RER stations, sewers and the foundations of buildings. At Paris Nord-Est, Magenta is already 30 m down. The model's illustration takes 35 m for all three stations assumption. That is within the range of stations that have been built, but it is not a design depth.

Depth does not strain the approaches. European rules allow tracks to slope by up to 35 mm per metre.18 A tunnel can therefore gain or lose 35 m of depth in one kilometre (derived). The portals are 4.5 to 7 km from the stations, and the stations 5 to 6 km from each other.

The Seine is crossed once, between Paris Nord-Est and Montparnasse. Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon are all on the right bank. Two lines already pass under the river in the centre: RER line B, on a ramp of 4%, and metro line 14 (unverified).40 30

From the hall to the coach

Deep platforms are further from the street than surface ones. But a terminal has its own long walk: the train stands beyond the gates, and the average coach is 200 m down the platform. A through station is entered from above, at several points along its length. Follow a passenger through both.

With platforms 35 m down, the deep station comes out at 4.0 minutes and the terminal at 3.7 minutes. The difference, about 18 seconds, is well inside the uncertainty of such a sketch. No measured times are published for the Paris terminals or for deep stations. The State's regional travel model applies a penalty to deep stations; its value is not published.42

What the model does with this

The central case takes the time inside the station as equal to today's. That is an assumption, and the result is sensitive to it: the sensitivity tests include two minutes more for every passenger, which removes 47% of the benefits.

Time inside the station is a separate matter from the time to reach its door. How long it takes to get from home or work to the entrance of a station where one's train stops is measured in reaching the station. The minutes on this page come on top, in both the present stations and the new ones.

How the station is run matters as much as how deep it is:

  • Today the platform is shown about 20 minutes before departure, and the gates close 2 minutes before.43 The passengers of a whole train, more than 1,000 when two sets are coupled, cross the hall in the same few minutes. SNCF tested showing platforms 30 minutes ahead in 2018.44
  • With fixed platforms, nobody waits for a screen. Passengers go down when they arrive and wait at the mark for their coach, as on Swiss platforms.45
  • Two stops spread the crowd. The passengers of one train from the south board at two stations, so each platform handles fewer people for each train.
  • The halls become waiting rooms. British design rules size a hall for the whole flow of the busiest quarter of an hour when the platform is announced late, and for a tenth of it when the platform is known in advance.41
  • London trains are the exception. Their passengers pass border checks first and keep a hall of their own, as described for Paris Nord-Est.

A benefit that is not counted: for trains that run every two hours or less often, the official method adds a 20-minute margin before departure.46 If fixed platforms let long-distance passengers arrive 5 minutes later, that would be worth about €223 million a year. No measurement exists of how early French passengers reach the station, so this stays out of the totals.

Chapter 4

Works, changes to today's stations, and stages

The stations would be built under four terminals that stay in use, and the tunnels under the city. This chapter shows how such works have been done elsewhere, what would change at each of today's stations, and how the project could open in two stages. The model assumes 12 years of works. That is an assumption, not a programme: there is no design and no ground investigation.

Four ways of building, all used before

Little can be dug from the street: the stations lie under working stations and the tunnels under buildings. Four methods have been used for works of this kind, in Paris or under a working terminal. Which one would serve where has not been studied.

1. A cavern dug from below

Workers reach the level of the station through a shaft, then dig the cavern from inside, a section at a time, and line it with concrete. Nothing is opened at the surface but the shafts.

  • Paris, Magenta and Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, 1999. Two stations of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Each is a central vault with two side vaults, 54 m and 58 m wide for four tracks, about 30 m down.19
  • At Magenta the ground was first strengthened with 3,570 columns of injected cement, and it still gave way once during the works.19
  • The line ended 44% above its approved cost. The review names the complexity of the project and the hazards of underground work.47

2. A box built from the top down, under working tracks

Walls are sunk from the surface and a roof is cast between them. Trains run again on the roof while the station is dug out underneath.

  • Zürich, Löwenstrasse, 2014. Four tracks 16 m under the terminal tracks,8 built between September 2007 and June 2014.48 8
  • Two or three tracks at a time, normally two, were shortened by 100 m; trains ran on all the others.49 50 Part of the roof and walls had been built in advance, when the platforms above were rebuilt.51
  • Under a listed wing of the station, 110 m were dug beneath the standing building; it settled 10 to 15 mm, with 25 mm allowed.52 See the Zürich annex.
  • Paris, Porte Maillot, 2024. Where nothing stands above, the box is simply dug open: 35 m deep, in 32 months.38

3. A station under a standing building

The building is first carried on new foundations. The station is then dug underneath it.

  • Paris, La Défense, 2024. The RER E station lies under an exhibition hall. Of the hall's 253 columns, 118 were moved onto about 1,800 small piles and a slab 3 m thick.53
  • The contract ran for 61 months.54 This station was under-estimated by €100 million, one of the named causes of the 45% overrun of the extension.55

4. Tunnels bored by machine

A cutting head as wide as the tunnel is lowered down a shaft. It digs forward and lines the tunnel with concrete rings behind it.

  • Paris, RER E extension, 2024. 8 km of tunnel 30 to 40 m deep, of which about 6 km in one tube 9.6 m wide inside for two tracks, with 10 shafts for air and rescue.17
  • London, Elizabeth line. Eight machines bored 42 km of tunnel between May 2012 and May 2015.56
  • Here: 100.5 km of two-track tunnel in layout A, 67.0 km in layout B, in six corridors of 4.5 to 7 km.

Method drawings illustrative sketch, not to scale.

None of these has been done at this size

The Paris caverns have four tracks and the Zürich box four. Paris Nord-Est would have 26 in layout A, under two terminals at once. The price of that step is the largest unknown in the cost.

Twelve years, year by year

An assumed schedule

The model assumes 12 years of works with even spending assumption. How those years divide between tasks and stages is an illustration made for this page. It is not a construction programme: there is no design, no ground investigation and no study of how many platforms each terminal can give up while it stays open.

Move through the years to see what is being built, what is open and what passengers find at each station.

Is twelve years plausible?

Smaller projects of the same kind took seven to thirteen years, and one is past twenty.

A longer schedule costs money as well as time, because interest runs during the works. Over 12 years it adds 20% to the cost. If the works took 15 years, the yearly cost of the project would rise by 4.0%; see the sensitivity tests.

Assumed here

  • 12 years of works, with even spending.
  • The first stage opens after year 9, the second after year 12.
  • Every terminal stays open until its deep station is ready.
  • The land is sold some years after the surface tracks close.

Not known

  • The design of any station, and so the method and time needed to build it.
  • The ground, the groundwater and the old quarries at each site.
  • How many platforms each terminal can give up during the works.
  • Where the shafts and work sites would go, and how the spoil would leave. At Zürich, up to three trains of spoil left the site each day.50
  • How long studies, public inquiry and approvals would take before the first year.
Chapter 5

Which trains run where

The same pattern of trains is assumed every hour. Every high-speed train stops at Paris Nord-Est; trains from the southeast also stop at Gare de Lyon, and trains from the Atlantic at Montparnasse. In a standard busy hour, 12 trains each way run straight through Paris and 6 each way pass from one southern line to the other by reversing at Nord-Est. That pattern, with room kept for the day the southern lines are full, sets the number of platforms.

One standard hour of high-speed trains

  • Every train stops at Paris Nord-Est. A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse, then at Nord-Est, then goes on. A train from Lille stops at Nord-Est, then at Gare de Lyon or at Montparnasse. So most trains stop twice in Paris, and every line meets every other at Nord-Est.
  • The same pattern every hour. The study assumes that the same trains run at the same minutes every hour. It has not drawn up a timetable, and the platform count below assumes that stops are spread through the hour. A timetable in which trains wait for each other at Nord-Est, as in Switzerland, is an option; it would need more platform tracks (see the Swiss timetable applied to Paris).
  • Platforms are fixed. The 14:07 to Lyon leaves from the same platform every day, printed in the timetable, with the place of each coach marked on the platform.45 What that changes for boarding is in the three stations.
  • High-speed trains are not for trips inside Paris. Tickets are sold from or to a station outside the region.

How many trains is a standard hour? This study takes 12 TGVs an hour each way on the Atlantic line, 12 on the southeast line, 8 on the northern line and 4 on the eastern line assumption. These are round numbers for a busy hour, not counts; the real pattern has to come from a timetable study (see what to verify). The second pattern below fills the two southern lines to their planned capacity: 16 trains an hour on the line to Lyon from 2030,15 and up to 15 on the Atlantic line with new signalling.4 68 No capacity figure was found for the northern and eastern lines; they are held at 8 and 4 assumption.

Any line can be paired with any other

The tunnels join all four lines at Nord-Est, so a train arriving from one line can leave by any of the others. The timetable is free to pair them as traffic requires, and to change the pairing from one hour to the next.

The four lines are not equal. The two southern lines carry more than twice the passengers of the northern and eastern ones: about 44 and 35 million a year counted at their Paris terminals, against 21.5 and 12 (derived).69 So not every train from the south can find a partner in the north or the east. In the standard hour, 4 trains from each southern line go on to the north and 2 to the east, which uses every train of the northern and eastern lines. The 6 trains left on each southern line are paired with each other.

For passengers, this gives direct trains on five of the six pairs of lines; only north to east has none. Crossing Paris by TGV gives the times for each pair.

If trains kept to fixed pairs

A simpler timetable would tie the southeast line to the north and the Atlantic line to the east, with no reversing. Direct trains would then exist on two pairs of lines only, and the project would add 2.3 million high-speed journeys a year instead of 2.6 million. The other tests are in what could change the answer.

The trains that reverse at Nord-Est

12trains an hour reverse at Nord-EstBoth directions together. 19 when the southern lines are full
8minallowed to change directionassumption A driver waits at the other end of the train. One more minute is counted for the train to clear the platform
29minfrom Montparnasse to Gare de LyonOn the train: 11 minutes to Nord-Est, 8 to reverse, 10 to Gare de Lyon
2.25stops' worth of platform timeA reversing train holds its platform 9 minutes (8 to reverse and 1 to clear), against 4 for a stop

A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse and at Nord-Est, changes direction there, stops at Gare de Lyon and continues to Marseille. This balances the four lines, and it gives direct trains between the Atlantic and the southeast, the largest flow across Paris.

  • How long it takes. A TGV needs 10 to 12 minutes to reverse at a platform, or about 3 with a second driver waiting at the other end.5 The estimate allows 8, and counts 9 minutes of platform time: one more for the train to clear the platform. The times between stations (10 and 11 minutes, stop included) are assumptions too.
  • What it costs. Platform time: reversals take up 53% of the platform time at Nord-Est in the standard hour. That is one reason why this station is the largest.
  • What it is worth to passengers. Less than a through run: 29 minutes in Paris against 11 for a train that runs straight through, but still about half of today's 57.5 minutes and with no change of train.
  • Other ways to handle the surplus remain open: sidings beside the high-speed depot 2 km north of Gare du Nord (unverified),59 or running on to the airport station at Roissy. Neither is costed here.

How many platforms

Through stations are planned for four to six long-distance trains an hour on each platform track. Stuttgart's new station, which is planned and not yet open, reached six in a simulated stress test,6 7 and the airport station at Roissy is rated at 8 trains an hour each way on its 4 tracks in theory.11 One station in service gives a measure: Zürich's Löwenstrasse station handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks,8 and through trains that wait for connections there stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).9 10 The rule used here: 5 stops of 4 minutes an hour on each track, so that a track is free two thirds of the time and a late train finds its platform. A train that reverses holds its platform for 9 minutes, 8 to change direction and 1 to clear, and counts as 2.25 stops. The stations are sized for the day the southern lines are full.

The sliders change the rule, not the timetable: more stops an hour on each track means less slack when trains run late.

Regional, suburban and London trains

  • Layout B shares the platforms. High-speed and regional express trains use the same tracks, as on the surface today: 20 at Nord-Est, 10 at Gare de Lyon and 8 at Montparnasse. That is two fewer at each station than the two groups have in layout A assumption. The two layouts are described in the project.
  • Regional express and suburban platforms are not worked out from a timetable: 6 and 4 tracks at Nord-Est, 4 and 2 at each southern station assumption. One imbalance needs attention: line H runs about four times as many trains as line R, its partner across Paris (476 against 120 a weekday, unverified).70 Most line H trains would turn back south of Gare de Lyon. The cost includes sidings for that.
  • London trains have two sealed tracks at Nord-Est with a hall of their own, counted on top of the tracks the rule gives (see Paris Nord-Est).
  • Depots stay where they are; trains reach them through the tunnel portals (see changes on the surface).
Chapter 6

How long to reach a station where your train stops

From the average point in Paris, a station where your TGV, the French high-speed train, stops is 27.4 minutes away today by public transport. With the three through stations it is 21.7 minutes to the nearest station where the train stops, or 26.1 minutes if the train’s ride between its Paris stops is counted, the measure used for benefits. The stations stay where they are and the project only adds places to board, so no point in Paris is further from its train than today, for any direction.

The map: 1,000 points in Paris

Each dot is a point in Paris. Its colour shows the time by public transport from the street to a station where a TGV for the chosen direction stops. Choose a view, a way of counting and a direction, then tap a dot to read its times.

    Tap or hover a dot to see, for each direction, where you board today and where you would board with the project.

    What “with the project” counts

    Today each direction has one terminal: Gare du Nord for the north, Gare de l’Est for the east, Gare de Lyon for the southeast, Montparnasse for the Atlantic. With the project every high-speed train stops at two or three stations in Paris, and a passenger boards at whichever suits best. Today’s station is always one of them. That is why the time can only get shorter.

    Trains forEvery train stops atHalf of the trains also stop at
    The north and the eastParis Nord-Est, entered from the Gare du Nord hall or from the Gare de l’Est hallGare de Lyon, for the half that come from the southeast; Montparnasse, for the half that come from the Atlantic
    The southeastGare de Lyon and Paris Nord-EstMontparnasse: these trains come from the Atlantic, change direction at Nord-Est and leave through Gare de Lyon
    The AtlanticMontparnasse and Paris Nord-EstGare de Lyon: these trains come from the southeast, change direction at Nord-Est and leave through Montparnasse

    Which trains run where is set out in how the lines are paired and trains that change direction. The even split between the two southern lines is an assumption, and so is free entry to Paris Nord-Est from both halls. The second one matters: with entry from the Gare du Nord side only, the Paris average on the stricter measure below would be 26.5 minutes and not 26.1, and people who live nearer to Gare de l’Est would be further from a train for the east than today.

    There are two honest ways to count the result. The map offers both.

    To the station entrance

    21.7 minutes on average, 5.7 fewer than today.

    The minutes by public transport from a point in Paris to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops. Where only half of the trains stop at the nearest station, the map takes the average of the two halves.

    This answers the plain question: how far am I from a station where my train stops? On this count 100% of the points are quicker than today, by up to 15.8 minutes.

    Counting the ride across Paris

    26.1 minutes on average, 1.3 fewer than today.

    The same, plus the train’s ride between its Paris stops when you board at the far one: 10 minutes between Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon, 11 between Nord-Est and Montparnasse, and 8 more when the train changes direction at Nord-Est assumption. You board at the far stop only when that still puts you ahead.

    This answers a stricter question: how much sooner am I on my way? It is the measure used for benefits. On this count 99% of the points are quicker, by up to 8.4 minutes, and the rest are unchanged.

    An example. Someone who lives near Montparnasse and travels to Lille crosses Paris by metro to Gare du Nord today. With the project, half of the Lille trains come up from the Atlantic and stop at Montparnasse first. The first measure counts only the short trip to Montparnasse. The second adds the 11 minutes the train takes to reach Nord-Est, because until then this passenger is no nearer to Lille than someone who boards at Nord-Est. Those minutes are spent in a seat on the right train and not in the metro, which is worth something, but they are still minutes.

    The model uses the stricter measure

    Every benefit and every extra passenger counted in this study comes from the second measure, the one that counts the train’s ride between its Paris stops. The first measure is shown because it is the one a passenger feels at the door. It is not used to count benefits.

    The map does not include the time inside the station, from the entrance to the coach, which is a separate matter treated in boarding in a deep station; the model also tests what happens if every passenger needs two more minutes than today, in the sensitivity tests.

    How the 1,000 times were computed. A grid of 1,000 points, 315 m apart, covers Paris without its two woods. From each point the model finds the shortest time to the hall of each station on foot, by metro, RER and tram, with the average wait for each line, on the network of Île-de-France Mobilités as of 5 October 2026.71 Buses, taxis and crowding are not counted. The four directions are weighted by their share of high-speed traffic: Atlantic 39%, southeast 31%, north 19%, east 11% (derived).69 The full method is in how access times are computed.

    Who gains, and what it is worth

    Every direction gains. At the station entrance the Atlantic and the southeast gain most, because all their trains would also stop at Nord-Est, on the other side of the city from their own station. Once the ride is counted the north gains most: a train for Lille boarded at Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse runs under Paris in 10 or 11 minutes, quicker than the metro.

    Minutes, Paris averageShare of trafficTodayTo the station entranceSaved at the entranceCounting the rideSaved with the ride
    North (Lille, London, Brussels)19%27.622.84.825.91.8
    East (Reims, Strasbourg)11%27.222.84.425.91.3
    Southeast (Lyon, Marseille)31%27.621.85.726.70.9
    Atlantic (Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes)39%27.120.86.325.81.3
    All directions, weighted by traffic100%27.421.75.726.11.3

    Even with the ride counted, the far stop is the better choice for a good part of Paris: for 16% of the points it is quicker to board a train for the southeast at Nord-Est than at Gare de Lyon, and for 22% it is quicker to board a train for the Atlantic at Nord-Est than at Montparnasse. For trains to the north, 12% of the points do better at Gare de Lyon and 20% at Montparnasse, on the trains that stop there.

    The north-east of Paris gains most. The 10th and 19th arrondissements (the districts of Paris) lie around and beyond Nord-Est, where every train would stop. Today their residents cross the city for a train to Lyon or Bordeaux. Their station entrance comes 12.2 and 12.1 minutes closer on average, or 4.9 and 4.9 minutes with the ride counted. The 18th follows with 9.7 and 3.0. The smallest gains are in the west: in the 8th and the 17th the entrance comes 2.1 and 2.3 minutes closer, and almost nothing changes once the ride is counted (0.3 and 0.2 minutes). These districts are about as far from one station as from another, so a second place to board helps them little.

    The numbers by arrondissement

    The suburbs gain a little more than Paris, because their trains and RER lines arrive on one side of the city. On the stricter measure the model finds 1.3 minutes saved for a trip that starts in Paris, 1.4 in the inner suburbs and 2.8 in the outer suburbs. The map shows Paris only.

    What quicker access is worth in the model

    The model counts the whole Paris region, on the stricter measure, in “equivalent minutes”: the official French method counts a minute of walking or changing as two and a minute of waiting as one and a half, because passengers dislike them more than sitting in a train.72 On that scale the average trip to the train is 2.3 minutes shorter.

    That is worth €137 million a year in time saved and brings about 1.1 million more high-speed journeys a year: British ticket data give about 11% more traffic for 10% less journey time.73

    Almost all of it comes from the choice of station. With the same three stations but each train boarded only at its own, the gain would be €27 million a year. The choice between two places to board is worth €110 million a year.

    These journeys are part of the high-speed traffic forecast, and the time saved is one line of the benefits.

    Chapter 7

    Crossing Paris, by TGV and by regional train

    A passenger who crosses Paris today spends about an hour between two trains, with a metro ride in the middle. With the stations joined, a direct train takes 10 to 29 minutes from one side of the city to the other, and a change of train happens on the platforms of one station. Suburban and regional passengers gain less on each trip, 2.3 minutes on the clock on average, but there are 115 million such journeys a year.

    TGV passengers who cross Paris

    About 107 million journeys a year by TGV, the French high-speed train, touch Paris: 102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it, changing between two Paris stations, usually by metro or by RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Those who cross are counted at two stations, which is why the four terminals count 112.5 million passengers. The 5.2 million is derived from the last survey, in 2012-13: 13,000 a day in the region, 88% of them in the stations inside Paris, all kinds of train together, scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since.2 No newer count is published, and none by pair of stations. The shares below assume that pairs follow the traffic of each station assumption.

    Atlantic and north21%57.5 min11 min23.5 min
    Southeast and north17%57.5 min10 min22.5 min

    Share of the passengers who cross Paris. Minutes in Paris, from arriving on one line to leaving on the other.

    • Five of the six pairs get direct trains in the standard hour described in which trains run where. A direct train does not suit every trip, so the estimate assumes that half of the passengers on those pairs find one for their own journey assumption. That makes 47% of all passengers who cross Paris; the others change inside Nord-Est.
    • North to east has no direct train. The two lines meet just north of the station, so a train from Lille would have to reverse at Nord-Est to leave for Strasbourg, and the plan already sends every train of these two lines on to the south. This is the smallest of the six flows. Passengers change on the platforms instead of walking between two stations.
    • What it is worth. €292 million a year in time saved, counted the official way, which weighs a minute spent changing as two minutes on a train.72 If every passenger on a served pair found a direct train the project would add 1.8 million journeys a year across Paris; if none did, 1.2 million. The central estimate is 1.5 million: see how many more passengers.
    • What is not known. The number of passengers itself. Counting all 13,000 of the survey, on more days of the year, gives 7.3 million instead of 5.2 million. Ticket data held by the operators would settle it.

    Regional and suburban passengers

    Suburban lines H, K, P, N and R and the regional express trains end at the four terminals today, unlike the RER. Run through, each train stops at a second station, and passengers stay on board when that station is nearer to where they are going.

    Lines H and K from the north run on to Gare de Lyon and join line R. Line P from the east runs on to Montparnasse and joins line N. Regional express trains do the same: those from the north and east continue to Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse, those from the south to Nord-Est.

    Trains are assumed to take 6 to 7 minutes between two stations assumption. The saving for each passenger is the difference between the trip from the old terminal to their destination in Paris and the trip from whichever of the two stops is nearer, measured on the public transport network as in reaching the station.

    The numbers as a table

    Million journeys a year. The total saves 2.3 minutes on average.

    115 million journeys a year save 2.3 minutes on the clock on average, and more with the official weights on walking and waiting, which is how the value of €129 million a year is counted.72 For line H, about half of the saving comes from being able to enter Nord-Est by either of its two halls, the rest from the second stop.

    Why two minutes matter

    • Fewer people change onto the metro and the RER at the terminals. Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est together see 800,000 travellers a day.3 A commuter from the northern suburbs who works near Gare de Lyon no longer goes down to RER D at Gare du Nord: the train goes there.
    • Crowding counts. In a survey of Île-de-France passengers, a minute in a full metro weighed up to 1.39 times a minute in an uncrowded one when seated, and 1.55 when standing.74 The estimate carries the comfort gained at €35 million a year, in the proportion found in the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express.75 The relief of each metro line is not modelled.
    • Not counted: trips from one suburb to another across Paris, which become direct. They need the region's travel model. The traffic these lines could gain is in how many more passengers.

    Chapter 8

    What it would cost to build

    No design exists yet, so the cost is built from quantities (kilometres of tunnel, metres of platform) and from the prices of stations and tunnels that have been built. It comes to about €70 billion with separate tunnels for high-speed trains, or €55 billion if they share tunnels with regional express trains. The stations, not the tunnels, are the largest item.

    Why €1.0 million per metre. The evidence from Paris points two ways. The first RER E stations, Saint-Lazare and Magenta, have four tracks each in caverns 30 m down, like the ones needed here. The whole 1999 line cost €2.5 billion in today's money; with its 4 km of tunnel deducted at our price, the stations come to about €0.9 million per metre, everything included (derived).47 The two-track stations opened in 2024 cost €0.9 million to €1.4 million per metre for their structure alone, before fit-out.17 53 The price used sits between them: it leans high against the one complete Paris figure and low against London. With design, client costs, land and risk, a metre of platform track is carried at €1.65 million.

    Not priced separately: the caverns at each end of a station where two tracks fan out into many. They are taken as covered by the station price, as in a French study of a four-track deep station whose box is 938 m long for 365 m of platform.37 For a station of 26 tracks this is untested.

    Try other prices

    Move the prices within what built projects show. The total and the yearly repayment follow. The repayment is what the capital account has to find each year.

    Result

    Does the method hold?

    The same prices were applied to seven projects that have been built or priced, and compared with their published cost.

    • Paris, built. The prices overshoot the first RER E section (3.2 against 2.5 before risk) and undershoot the 2024 extension (4.6 against 5.8 to 7.1). With the 30% allowance the extension is matched at the low reading of its cost and still missed at the high one.
    • France, study estimates. Before risk, the prices come close to what SNCF Réseau itself estimates for a deep four-track station with its tunnels: 3.5 against 3.8 for Lyon, 3.9 against 3.4 for Marseille, a figure that covers a whole phase of works. Those estimates carry a contingency of their own, and in Paris such estimates have run 45% over.
    • Abroad. Stuttgart falls inside the range (12.6 to 16.4 against 14.5, which is in money of each year and would be higher in 2026 euros). Zürich cost much less than the prices give. Munich, with stations 40 m under the centre, is costing twice as much.
    The reading

    The prices are those of a French study estimate, and the 30% is what it takes to reach what such projects end up costing. It is not a cushion. The spread between Zürich and Munich is the real uncertainty.

    The cost per year

    To compare a cost paid once with money and benefits that come every year, the construction cost is turned into a yearly repayment, like a loan repaid over 60 years at 3% above inflation. Money is spent for years before the first train runs: over 12 years of even spending assumption, interest during the works adds 20%. Each €1 billion of construction then costs €43 million a year.

    Running the tunnels and stations. Two French records exist. The first RER E section cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, for two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel; maintenance of the structures alone was six times the forecast.47 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track to maintain, about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.86 Stations are taken at the first figure and tunnels midway between the two, €2.25 million per km assumption. The range, and what it does to the accounts, is in the operations account.

    The State borrows long-term at 5.4% in October 2026, inflation included.87 The saving from closing the surface platforms and tracks is not deducted. Running high-speed trains is left to their operators.

    Chapter 9

    How many more passengers

    The project would add about 2.6 million high-speed journeys a year and 21 million suburban and regional ones. Both figures rest on what was counted in cities that joined their terminals, and on a model of time saved where no count exists. They are small against today's traffic, and a charge on passengers of the TGV, the French high-speed train, would take away more high-speed journeys than the project adds.

    What other cities saw

    Many cities have joined suburban lines through their centre and counted the passengers afterwards. For long-distance trains the record is thin: no railway has published its passengers before and after a terminal became a through station.

    • The best cases gained 24% to 30% within one to three years. Stockholm's commuter trains gained 26% in two years while the rest of the network gained 3%.97 Zürich gained 24% in the first year of its 1990 through station, with twice the trains.98 Tokyo's Fukutoshin line gained 30% in six months.96
    • Others gained little. Line E of the Paris RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground, has gained about 10% so far on 30% more service.101 St. Gallen ran 25% more trains for 5% more travel.102 Philadelphia joined its two networks in 1984 during a collapse of service and saw no gain for ten years (unverified).103
    • Where a whole new line came with it, traffic multiplied, mostly by moving passengers. London's Elizabeth line carries four times its predecessor services.104 105 Only 9% to 10% of its journeys are new to public transport.106 In Sydney the figure is 27%.107 The annex on the Elizabeth line has the detail.

    Reading. A second stop in the city draws a real share of passengers, and removing a change of station is worth far more than the minutes it saves. But no case isolates the effect of a through station on long-distance traffic. That is why this study leans on British ticket data and on a model of time saved.

    Suburban and regional trains: 15% more on the joined lines

    Used here: 15% more journeys on the five suburban lines assumption. The eight cases above average 16%, before deducting growth that would have come anyway, and the Paris lines would be joined with little extra service. On 132 million journeys a year that is 20 million more. The low and high cases take 5% and 25%: 6.6 and 33.1 million.

    • Regional express trains. No case exists for trains whose trips are long. The time model is used instead: traffic rises about 11% when the whole journey gets 10% shorter.73 A second stop saves 2.4 to 3.4 weighted minutes on a trip taken as 100 minutes door to door assumption, which gives 3.6%, or 1.5 million journeys on 41 million.
    • A new journey is not always a new customer. Most of the growth seen elsewhere came from people who already used public transport. The financing chapter takes 30% of the extra suburban journeys as made by new holders of a Navigo pass, the travel pass of the region assumption: €14 million a year. New regional express passengers bring €12 million in fares. Together that is €26 million a year, a small sum (see more Navigo pass holders).
    • New lines take years to fill. Paris's RER D opened at 58% of its forecast and was at 84% eight years later; RER E opened at 53%.47 The figures here are for a mature service.

    High-speed trains: two modest gains

    Two groups of TGV passengers gain from the project, and each is estimated in its own way.

    Starting or ending in the Paris region

    102 million journeys a year today. With two stops in Paris for most trains, the station where the train stops is nearer for most travellers: 2.3 minutes nearer on average, with walking and waiting counted at their official weights (see reaching the station).

    The time model turns that into traffic: about 11% more for a journey 10% shorter.73 Result: 1.1 million more journeys, a gain of 1.1%.

    Crossing Paris

    5.2 million journeys a year today (derived, see crossing Paris). For the 47% who would find a direct train, a gain of 37% is taken, from British ticket data on what a change of train costs (see below).73 For the others, who still change but inside one station, the time model is used.

    Result: 1.5 million more journeys, a gain of 29%.

    Why 37%. The British paper finds that adding a change of train loses 37% of passengers in the long run, on routes of about 100 miles.73 This study takes 37% as the gain when a change is removed assumption. That is cautious: the same finding read the other way gives about 59%, since a flow that has lost 37% gains that much when it comes back. This is near the 57% of the Paris bypass line, whose services carried that much more than they would have without it (derived), new stations and time savings included.108 The high case uses the bypass figure: 2.0 million journeys. The low case drops the British figure and keeps the time model alone: 1.4 million. Two differences remain: the British routes had their change inside one station, where Paris has a change of station, and French high-speed trips are much longer.

    Small numbers, and a charge that would cancel the TGV gain

    107millionhigh-speed journeys a year touch Paris102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it. Those who cross are counted at two stations, hence 112.5 million passengers counted at the four terminals (derived for 2024)69
    +2.4%high-speed journeys2.6 million more, before any charge
    +12%suburban and regional journeys21.3 million more on 173 million; 5% to 20% in the low and high cases
    -0.3 to -1.5millionhigh-speed journeys, net of the charge2.6 million gained, 2.9 to 4.1 million lost to a charge of €2.55 per departure or arrival

    About 107 million high-speed journeys a year touch Paris. The project changes how they begin, end or cross the city, but it creates few new ones: 2.6 million, a gain of 2.4%. The trains do not run faster and the fares do not fall; a station is a little nearer, and the 5% of travellers who cross Paris no longer change station.

    The financing of the project looks to those same passengers. The passenger charge tested there is €2.55 on each high-speed departure or arrival in Paris and €5.10 for a passenger who crosses the city, on an average fare of €48.50. French experts take TGV traffic to fall by 0.5% to 0.7% when fares rise by 1%.118 With a response of 0.5 to 0.7, the charge would remove 2.9 to 4.1 million journeys a year, against 2.6 million added: a net change of -0.3 to -1.5 million. A charge of about €1.59 to €2.25 would lose as many journeys as the project adds.

    What this means

    The case for the project cannot rest on new high-speed traffic. It rests on the time saved by people who already travel, worth about €429 million a year to high-speed passengers and €129 million to suburban and regional ones, on the land freed on the surface and, outside this estimate, on room for more trains later. The economic return adds these up, and what could change the answer tests each assumption of this chapter.

    Chapter 10

    Paying to run it, paying to build it

    The money is kept in two accounts. Running the tunnels and stations would cost about €0.64 billion a year; a charge of €2.55 on each high-speed passenger and the other income found here cover 56% to 72% of it, and between half and all of it across what running costs could turn out to be. Repaying construction costs €2.39 billion to €3.06 billion a year and nothing the project earns reaches that: it has to come from taxes and grants, as for most comparable tunnels.

    Two accounts

    Two words first: TGV is the French high-speed train, and RER the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. An operations account holds what it costs each year to keep the tunnels and stations open, and what the project earns each year. A capital account holds the repayment of construction, spread over 60 years like a loan, and the taxes and grants assigned to it. Keeping them apart answers two different questions: can the project pay its own way once built, and who pays to build it.

    The hope behind this split was that operations would pay for themselves and that the added economic activity would repay construction. The first is within reach and not yet shown: with a €2.55 charge, income covers 56% of running costs for layout A and 72% for layout B, and layout B balances if running costs are at the low end of the evidence. The second does not hold on the figures of this study: the benefits counted for the country are worth 28% to 36% of the yearly repayment of construction (see the economic return).     The running cost is the least certain figure

    Two French records exist, and they are far apart.

    • The first RER E section (two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel, opened in 1999) cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, several times its forecast: 8.7 for maintenance of the infrastructure, 9.2 for operating the stations, 3.4 for guarding and utilities.47 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The index is a choice: no official index exists for running costs, and consumer prices have risen less.
    • The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track a year to maintain, so about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.86
    • Used here: stations at the RER E rate; tunnels at €2.25 million per km, midway between the two assumption. The low case takes tunnels at the RER network rate and stations at 70% of the RER E rate; the high case takes both from the RER E record.
    • Gross, not net. The new stations replace terminals whose staff, cleaning and energy are paid for today. That saving is not deducted, because it has not been measured. It would lower the cost again.
    • The level of the charge. In the central case operations balance at €6.15 per departure or arrival for layout A and €4.29 for layout B; at the low end of running costs, at €3.52 and €2.40; at the high end, at €7.88 and €5.38. A higher charge loses more passengers.
    • More sources. Those that could be negotiated add about €91 million a year.
    • What to ask first. The track owner and the station operator hold the real running costs of RER E, of the stations opened in 2024 and of today's terminals. They decide whether this account balances.

    For comparison: fares cover 37% of the running of public transport in the Paris region (derived)121 and 64% in the Zürich network.122 The Elizabeth line earned £731 million in fares against £554 million of running costs in 2025 to 2026, trains included;105 it keeps its fares. Here the fares of high-speed trains belong to their operators and suburban fares to the region, which is why the project needs a charge of its own.

    A charge on high-speed passengers

    The proposal tested: every TGV ticket to or from Paris carries €2.55, the price of a metro ticket in 2026.123 A passenger who arrives in Paris and leaves on another train pays it twice. A passenger who crosses Paris on a direct train pays €5.10. The reasoning is that passengers from the Paris region gain a choice of stations, and passengers who cross Paris gain a great deal of time.

    What it brings. About 107 million high-speed journeys a year touch Paris: 102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it. After the loss of traffic described below, the charge collects €286 million a year. The track owner loses the charges it collects on the journeys given up, which leaves €216 million.

    What it costs in traffic. €2.55 is 5% on an average fare of €48.5 before VAT. French experts take traffic to fall 0.7% when fares rise 1%, perhaps 0.5% where prices already vary with demand, as they do on TGVs.118 On that basis the charge loses 2.9 million to 4.1 million journeys a year. The project adds 2.6 million. With this charge, high-speed traffic through Paris ends 0.3 million to 1.5 million journeys lower than today.

    Why. The gain is uneven. A passenger who crosses Paris saves about 34 minutes on the clock. The official method counts a change at twice its length, which makes 84 minutes, worth about €49: far more than €5.10. A passenger from the Paris region gains 1.6 minutes on the clock on average, counted as 2.3 with the official weights on walking and waiting, worth about €1.33: less than the charge. And there are twenty times more of the second kind.

    A variant that follows the gains. Charging €1.30 per departure or arrival and €15 for a direct crossing keeps traffic at today's level (change of 0.0 million journeys) but collects €180 million instead of €286 million. The volume is in Paris trip ends, so any design must choose between money and traffic. Both variants can be tried in the calculator.

    Is it possible in law? Two routes exist. Station charges are regulated at cost plus a return: €1,260 million a year for all French stations in 2026.124 The cost of the new stations would enter that base and be billed to train operators, who pass it on. European law also lets a track owner charge more for a specific project, on the basis of its long-term cost.125 The other route is a levy written into a budget law, as for the airport express, repaid in part by a levy on air passengers.126 127 Precedents for the level: the solidarity tax on a flight from Paris within Europe is €7.40;128 operators pay the Channel Tunnel about €35 per passenger (derived, upper bound).129 The figures here take the charge as free of VAT; if it carried the 10% VAT of tickets, the project would keep €2.32 of each €2.55.

    More Navigo pass holders

    Navigo is the travel pass of the Paris region. Joining the suburban lines through Paris should bring new regular users: the model expects 19.9 million more suburban journeys a year (see regional traffic). A pass costs €998.80 a year whatever the number of trips,123 so a pass holder who travels more brings nothing. What counts is how many people buy a pass because of the project.

    The estimate. A regular commuter makes about 420 rail journeys a year assumption. If 30% of the new journeys are made by new pass holders assumption, that is about 14,200 passes and €14 million a year. The share is the unknown. Where it has been measured on new through lines, the share of journeys that are new to public transport was 9% to 10% in London,106 27% in Sydney (derived)107 and 28% to 32% on the East London line;130 the figure used here is at the top of that range.

    How to measure it. Count passes and validations on lines H, K, P, N and R before and after opening, and compare with lines that did not change. Passes are registered to a home address, so new holders along the joined lines can be counted directly. The regional authority's budget attributes no revenue to new lines today;121 an agreement would have to say that the measured gain is paid to the project.

    Its weight. Small either way. Fares bring the region €4.2 billion a year,121 and the project adds a few tens of millions at most. The extra running of the trains, €55 million a year, is charged to the project in the same account.

    • Land comes late and once. It is sold after the surface tracks close, and its area has never been measured.

    What the country gets back

    Most of what the project returns never passes through a ticket gate: time saved by passengers of the TGV (the French high-speed train) and of regional trains, more comfortable journeys, a larger job market. Counted with the official French values, these benefits are worth €0.86 billion a year, 23% to 30% of the yearly cost. Comparable tunnels were approved with benefits between half and twice their cost. As counted here, this project is below that range, and this chapter shows what is missing.

    What public budgets get back

    Added activity pays taxes, and part of the public money spent returns to public budgets. This can be estimated, in three layers that must be kept apart because they do not have the same standing. The answer depends above all on one question that this study cannot settle: how much of the activity added around the stations is new for the country, and how much is moved from elsewhere.

    • Layer 1: money that reaches the Treasury because of the project. Tickets carry 10% VAT, which businesses cannot recover.147 It applies to the net change in ticket money. With the charge, high-speed traffic does not rise, so this layer is about zero; the charge itself is taken as free of VAT. VAT lost on what passengers stop buying elsewhere is not deducted. Experience elsewhere is that this layer can be negative: the evaluation of High Speed 1 found a loss of tax of over £0.8 billion, because rail travel is taxed less than what it replaces.144
    • Layer 2: tax on added activity. France takes 43.6% of its output in taxes and social contributions.148 The rate is not in doubt; what is in doubt is how much of a local gain is new for the country. British guidance starts from the assumption that none is, unless the project is shown to bring more people into work.149 150 That is the first column. The middle column takes the wider effects as the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express counts them: each extra job is valued there at €10,000 a year of unemployment benefits saved,75 which is itself a public saving; output from denser job markets and from working time saved (for the 30% of TGV passengers who travel for work, unverified151) is taxed at 43.6%. The last column supposes that the 14,200 jobs implied are all new and each pays tax on the average output of a job in the region, €123,220.152
    • Layer 3: tax returned by the works. A simulation by the French economic observatory finds that 40% to 60% of debt-financed public investment returns to public budgets within five years, through wages, profits and lower benefits.153 This is real cash for the Treasury while the works last. It is not a gain from this project: any spending of the same size would return the same.
    How official appraisal treats taxes

    The French method does not count taxes as a benefit. It counts each euro of public money at €1.20, because raising taxes has a cost of its own, and it leaves out jobs created by the works and multiplier effects to avoid counting twice.154 The builder of the Grand Paris Express claimed up to €4 billion of tax a year for output of €10 billion to €20 billion; the State's reviewers did not endorse a tax line.155 75 For Crossrail, consultants put tax at 27% to 29% of added output.156 The table above is therefore a view for public finances, beside the appraisal and not inside it.

    The reading. Between nothing and about €840 million a year comes back, €220 million on the middle reading: 7% of the repayment of layout A and 9% of layout B. On the most generous reading it is 27% and 35%. Tax receipts lower the net cost for public budgets; on no reading do they repay construction.

    Against comparable projects

    The measure used everywhere is the ratio of benefits to costs over the life of the project, both brought to today's value. Above 1, the country gets back more than it spends. The ratios below are not strictly comparable, and the differences cut both ways:

    What the comparison says

    • On transport benefits alone, cross-city tunnels rarely return much more than their cost. Published ratios at approval run from about 0.5 to 2. Five of the thirteen stand below 1 on those benefits; they were built or are promoted for capacity, or rest on wider effects: Stockholm, Malmö, Gothenburg, Lucerne, the Grand Paris Express.
    • Wider effects decide the largest projects. They are a fifth to a third of the benefits in London, Sydney and Melbourne, and about 60% for the Grand Paris Express.
    • Measured returns are usually lower than forecast. High Speed 1 went from 1.5 to 0.64, Stockholm from 0.86 to 0.51, RER E from 21% to about 10%.
    • This project is below all of them as counted here, on any of the bases above. It costs more than any of them and its counted benefits are those of a mid-sized scheme. Either the count misses its main purpose, capacity for more trains, or the project is too large for what it delivers. Telling the two apart is the first job of a study.

    What would have to be true

    Could the benefits reach the cost? Not in any case tested. Each step below adds one favourable assumption to the one before.

    Closing the rest would take benefits that are not counted here. Three could be large enough, and each can be checked:

    1. Capacity. If the terminals are what stops more trains from running, the project should be credited with the traffic it unlocks. For scale: each 10% of extra high-speed traffic is 11 million journeys and €546 million of tickets a year, 15% to 19% of the yearly cost. Even counted in full, the gap of the central case would take about 37% more traffic for layout B, against 29% more trains planned on the southern lines. This needs the view of the track owner, SNCF Réseau, of when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project.
    2. The regional network. The count for suburban passengers rests on an average saving of 2.3 minutes and on ratios borrowed from another project. The region's travel model would show suburb to suburb trips, relief of the RER, and a real figure for wider effects.
    3. Cost. Stations at the Zürich price would cut the cost of layout A by 20%. Whether Paris ground and 400 m trains allow it is an engineering question.

    The tests that move the result most are in risks and next steps; the same levers can be moved by hand in the financing calculator.

    Chapter 12

    What could change the answer, and what to verify

    The case rests on a handful of things nobody has yet measured or drawn. Cost and the time needed to board in a deep station move the economic result most; the level of running costs decides whether the project can pay its own way once open. Most of these can be settled by studies that cost little next to the project.

    How sure is the result?

    Each line changes one assumption and shows the share of the yearly cost that all the benefits counted then cover. The central case is 24% for layout A and 30% for layout B. These tests are run without the passenger charge, which changes the figures by less than one point. Tests that change only the project's income, such as more trains once the terminals are relieved, are in the financing chapter: more trains would bring ticket money and track charges, but the benefit of the extra journeys is not valued here, which is why the case for capacity is still to be made (see what would have to be true).

    • Cost matters most. The same benefits cover 17% to 44% of the cost depending on prices and layout.
    • Boarding time comes next. Two minutes more for every passenger removes 47% of the benefits: an extra 1.1 minutes on the clock is enough to cancel the whole gain in access. This is why the design of the Nord-Est station is the first thing to study (see inside the station).
    • Growth over time counts. Benefits are held flat in the central case. If they grow 1.5% a year, as values of time and traffic usually do, they are worth 1.41 times more over 60 years assumption.
    • The money side has its own tests. Running costs, the level of the charge and the response of passengers to it are tested in the operations account and can be moved in the calculator.

    Stages and the decision

    The project can be built in two stages: first the north to southeast axis with Paris Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon (€50 billion for layout A), then Montparnasse and the Atlantic (€21 billion); see works and stages. The first stage serves the trains of three of the four high-speed lines. Its benefits on its own have not been estimated, so this study cannot say whether stopping after it would be a better or a worse project.

    What to decide now

    Not whether to build. The decision today is whether to spend on five quick tests that can confirm or stop the case:

    1. Ask for ticket data on passengers who change station in Paris, by origin and destination (study point C1).
    2. Draw one standard hour of trains with the track owner (SNCF Réseau), including trains that reverse at Nord-Est (A1, A2).
    3. Commission a concept design of the Nord-Est station: position, depth, time from hall to train, and a first engineer's price (A4, B2).
    4. Ask what deep stations and tunnels cost to run, from the records of RER E and of the stations opened in 2024 (B5). Whether the project can pay its own running costs turns on it.
    5. Ask when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project (C6). The economic case turns on it, and it is not valued in this study.

    With those in hand, choose between layouts A and B (A7), settle the level and the legal form of the passenger charge (D7), and take the case to a full appraisal.

    The case in three sentences
    • It serves passengers better than today, and nobody is further from a train than before.
    • It does not pay for itself. With a charge of €2.55 on each high-speed passenger, income covers 56% to 72% of running costs, perhaps all of them for layout B, and none of the construction; the benefits counted are worth 23% to 30% of the yearly cost.
    • It is a public investment, to be judged like the Grand Paris Express: on room for the next century's trains and on the city it leaves behind. Those are the benefits this study could not count, and the case stands or falls on them. It is strongest for layout B.
