    Annex A

    Zürich: a terminus that became a through station

    Zürich's main station was a terminus: 16 tracks ending at buffer stops in the middle of the city. Rather than enlarge it, the canton twice built a four-track through station underneath, in 1990 and in 2014, each with its own tunnel. The eight through tracks are under a third of the station's platform tracks and carry, on a rough count, close to half of its trains.

    Four stations in one

    Zürich Hauptbahnhof is four stations on one site: the surface hall, two underground through stations on its north and south edges, and a small terminus for two local lines under the forecourt. A level of passages and shops ties them together. The S-Bahn, named throughout, is the suburban rail network of the Zürich region. Choose a year to see the station grow, and a part to read what it is, when it opened, what it cost and which trains use it.

    Parts of the station

    The hall

    • What: 16 dead-end tracks on the surface, numbered 3 to 18, under a train shed of 1933, with seven island platforms and two side platforms.172 Track 3 is the southern edge and track 18 the northern edge.173
    • Platforms: lengthened to 420 m in 2002 to 2004.50
    • Trains: long-distance trains that end here or turn back, international trains and four S-Bahn lines.174 About 18 of the 27 long-distance departures in one hour of 2026 (derived).10
    • Before 1989: the tracks were numbered 1 to 16.172

    Passages and shops

    • What: four passages run north to south under the hall tracks. Three of them form one complex with the shops under the forecourt.174 Its two halls lie 4.7 m and 7.3 m below ground.172
    • Dates: first shops in 1970, enlarged in 1990 and 2014.172 The westernmost passage was widened from about 10 m to about 35 m in 2005 to 2008, with a lift and escalators to each platform, for CHF 56.8 million.51 175
    • Why it matters: the passages join both underground stations to each other and to the hall.8 The station's standard minimum time for a change is 7 minutes.176

    The river Sihl

    • What: the river crosses the station under the tracks in five culverts about 190 m long, each about 12 m wide and 3 m high. The bridges that carry the 16 tracks are the roof of the culverts.177
    • Under it: the roof of Löwenstrasse station lies about 1 m below the river bed,177 and its tracks 11 m below the river.51
    • During the works: two of the five culverts were dried at a time, in four stages from April 2008 to December 2010, while the river ran in the other three. The site was to be cleared and flooded if a large flood was forecast.51

    Museumstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 41 to 44, on two island platforms 360 m long, 13.6 m below the street of the same name on the north side.172
    • Opened: May 1989 for a few regional trains,172 and 27 May 1990 for the S-Bahn.178
    • Trains: S-Bahn only, 11 lines.174 Up to 20 trains an hour each way at the peak.98 Stadelhofen, the next station on the same lines, sees 770 trains a day.179
    • Cost: part of the line of 1990, CHF 866 million in all.180

    Tunnels to the east

    • What: the Hirschengraben tunnel, 2.1 km underground of which 1.3 km bored, leads to Stadelhofen station; the Zürichberg tunnel, 5.0 km, carries on to the suburbs.181 182 About 12 km of new line in all.98
    • Opened: 27 May 1990, after nine years of works.178
    • Cost: CHF 866 million with Museumstrasse station, of which the canton paid 80%.180
    • Today's limit: Stadelhofen has three tracks and is described as the largest bottleneck of the S-Bahn. A fourth track with second tunnel tubes is planned for 2027 to 2037 at CHF 1.1 billion.179

    SZU terminus

    • What: two dead-end tracks, 21 and 22, with one island platform 125 m long, 11.6 m below the forecourt.172 SZU is a separate local railway.
    • Opened: 5 May 1990. It uses a section built ahead for an underground railway that voters rejected in 1973.183 184
    • Cost: a credit of CHF 72.4 million, approved by 67% of voters in 1983.184
    • Trains: two local lines, to the Sihl valley and to the Uetliberg, about seven trains an hour.183

    Sihlpost wing station

    • What: four extra dead-end tracks, 51 to 54, on the surface south of track 3 and set back from the hall. In service from 2003, closed on 15 June 2014 and removed.173
    • Trains: the S-Bahn lines S1, S2, S8 and S14, which turned back here.185
    • Why: it freed hall tracks for the national timetable of 2004. The government accepted it only as an unavoidable stopgap: it met broad opposition because of longer changes and worse access to the city centre.185

    Löwenstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 31 to 34, on two island platforms 420 m long and 13.5 m wide, 16 m below hall tracks 4 to 9.8 50 The whole structure is 675 m long.8
    • Opened: 15 June 2014 for the S-Bahn, 13 December 2015 for long-distance trains.186 187
    • Cost: CHF 674 million for the station.81
    • Trains: 460 a day, of which 140 long-distance and 320 S-Bahn.8 In 2026: four Intercity lines between western and eastern Switzerland, one regional express and the trains to Munich.10
    • Built under the working hall: its roof and walls were laid in 2002 to 2004, when the platforms above were being rebuilt anyway.51 See the lessons.

    Weinberg tunnel

    • What: 4.8 km, two tracks in one tube more than 11 m across, from the east end of Löwenstrasse station to Oerlikon.8 It passes under the river Limmat and 5 m below the Hirschengraben tunnel, then turns through about 180 degrees to reach Oerlikon from the south.188
    • Built: main drive from June 2010, breakthrough on 22 November 2010.189 Opened with the station on 15 June 2014.186
    • Cost: CHF 498 million.81
    • Trains: 12 S-Bahn trains an hour each way at opening.186 Main station to airport in 9 minutes by Intercity.190

    Bridges to the west

    • What: two bridges, 1,156 m and 394 m long, carry the new line in from Altstetten, to the west.8 A ramp leads down to the station; the approaches slope at up to 37 mm per metre.189
    • Opened: December 2015. Long-distance trains have run through the station since then.8 187
    • The whole line: 9.6 km from Altstetten to Oerlikon.191

    Details cited to Wikipedia in these descriptions are unverified: the layout of the hall and the lines that use each part, the sizes and depths of Museumstrasse station and of the SZU terminus, the levels and dates of the passages, the lengths and route of the tunnels, the figures for Stadelhofen, the dates of the wing station and the vote of 1983.

    Why through platforms, and not a bigger terminus

    Twice the first plan was something else, and twice voters chose a through station by a large majority.

    YearWhat happened
    1973Voters reject a credit of CHF 599 million for an underground railway with an S-Bahn: 57% no.184
    1981They approve CHF 523 million for the S-Bahn alone, with a through station under the north edge of the main station: 74% yes.184 180
    1990The line opens after nine years of works.178 On a working day, S-Bahn traffic at the city boundary is 24% higher in the first year.98
    1990sFor the national timetable of 2004, the railway plans a wing station beside the hall for four S-Bahn lines, and two more tracks on the viaduct towards Oerlikon: about CHF 650 million, plus CHF 200 million to CHF 300 million further out.192 193
    1997 to 1998Residents of two city districts resist the wider viaduct, and the canton's heritage and noise offices oppose it.50 194
    1999A popular initiative, "For a through station, no wing station", asks for a tunnel and an underground through station. The government answers with a proposal of its own and the initiative is withdrawn.195
    2001Over 80% of the canton's voters (82% in the engineering press) approve CHF 580 million, the canton's 40% share of an estimate of CHF 1,450 million.175 52 195
    2003The wing station opens all the same, as a stopgap, and closes the day the through station opens in 2014.173

    The vote shares of 1973 and 1981 and the dates of the wing station are from Wikipedia and unverified; the canton confirms the date and the amount of the vote of 1981.

    The reasons given at the time were not journey times first.

    1. The terminus could not grow where it stood. The government found the scope to develop the station at its site and level "severely limited". A new main station on another site was examined and dropped.185
    2. The bottleneck was the line out, not only the platforms. Towards Oerlikon and the airport, more trains were "hardly possible". A through station joined to a new pair of tracks was called "the key element".185
    3. The wing station put passengers too far from their connections. The initiative called the walk from there to the express trains unacceptable; a through station under the hall gives "the most direct connections to the other tracks".185
    4. Turning back wastes platforms and tracks. The trade press called it "a time waster" and an "inefficient use of platform and track space".196 The canton listed the end of the reversal among the gains.197
    5. It was built for long trains from the start. The canton judged that the S-Bahn alone would never fill a second through station. Platforms of 420 m instead of 300 m cost just under CHF 30 million more.185

    The result, as stated by the engineers: four through tracks raised the capacity of the whole station by about one third.50 The gain was not published in trains per hour.

    How to read it. A through train that waits for connections still stands 6 to 9 minutes. Only a train that does not wait shows the bare stop of 3 minutes, and a train that turns back can leave after 5. So the length of the stop is set mainly by the connections, not by the reversal (derived). What the through station removes is the reversal itself, the crossing of other trains' paths on the way in and out, and several minutes of approach. Where a locomotive must be changed at a reversal, that alone takes 4.5 minutes.176

    What changed

    +1/3capacity of the whole stationFrom four more through tracks, as stated by the engineers50
    460trains a day under the hall140 long-distance and 320 S-Bahn at Löwenstrasse8
    1 in 3long-distance trains runs through9 of 27 departures and 8 of 25 arrivals in one hour of 2026 (derived)10 9
    6minsaved on the S-Bahn across the cityFrom Oerlikon through the main station to the left shore of the lake186

    Traffic. The first through station changed the S-Bahn most. On a working day, 159,288 passengers crossed the city boundary by S-Bahn in the year before it opened, 196,854 in the first year after, and 445,562 in November 2014: 180% more in 24 years, with twice as many trains an hour at the peak.98 From 2014 to 2019, with the second through station, S-Bahn traffic grew by a further 19%.99 How much of this growth is due to the stations themselves cannot be separated from the growth of the region and of the service.

    Trains. The station handled about 1,400 trains a day around 2000 and about 2,000 in 2007.203 48 Around 2020 it handled 2,915 train movements a day, of which 2,607 passenger trains (unverified).173

    Journeys. S-Bahn trains cross the city about 6 minutes faster and long-distance trains up to 7 minutes faster; the main station is 9 minutes from the airport.186 204 190 A few journeys became longer.

    Journey by journey: seven examples, including those that lost
    JourneyWhat the cross-city line changed
    S-Bahn, Oerlikon to Altstetten11 minutes, with five direct trains an hour each way instead of one.197
    S-Bahn, Oerlikon to Enge, south of the centreUp to 40% shorter.197
    Long-distance trains through ZürichUp to 7 minutes faster, as expected by SBB in 2013.204
    Zürich to St. Gallen18 minutes shorter in December 2015, with three trains an hour instead of two. The saving combined the end of the reversal with dropped stops.187 In 2026 the fastest trains take 58 to 60 minutes and that non-stop pattern no longer runs.205

    Some loseThe Basel to airport train, now routed through the main station, takes about 10 minutes between Altstetten and Oerlikon instead of 6 to 7.197 Passengers of one local line wait about 15 minutes longer for long-distance trains; the government answered that perfect connections for all would cost too much.207

    Cost. The line of 1990 cost CHF 866 million in the final account. The canton paid CHF 693 million, 80% of it: CHF 14 million less than its credit of CHF 523 million once CHF 69 million of approved extra works and CHF 114 million of inflation were added.180 The cross-city line of 2014 and 2015 was put to voters at CHF 1,450 million at 2000 prices.195 Its final account is CHF 2,052 million at 2005 prices, 1% above the ceiling of CHF 2,031 million agreed in 2008; the canton paid one third and the Confederation two thirds.81 In this study's 2026 euros the line comes to about €2.75 billion.

    Punctuality: no figure is published for Zürich before and after the through stations. The regional transport authority states that the main station now has enough capacity for the growth expected in the foreseeable future and that timetable stability improved across Switzerland.8

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What carries over

    • Put the through tracks where the trains already are. Both new stations lie under the old hall or right beside it, and one level of passages serves all of them. The wing station beside the hall was accepted only as a stopgap, because of the walk.
    • A few through tracks do a lot. Four of them added about a third to the capacity of the whole station.50
    • Build for long trains at once. Platforms of 420 m were a small extra cost, and they are why Intercity trains use the station today.
    • It can be built under a working station. The roof slab, walls and columns went in first, from the surface; the station was then dug out under the slab. Normally two hall tracks at a time (two to three in the engineering press) were shortened by 100 m, leaving about 300 m of platform in use, and trains kept running on all the other tracks.49 50 The listed south wing of the station building was underpinned and settled by 10 to 15 mm, against 25 mm allowed.52 For Paris, see building methods.
    • The cost held once the works were let, not before. The second project ended 1% above the ceiling agreed in 2008, but that ceiling was 40% above the estimate put to voters in 2001, in prices five years older.81 195

    Where the comparison stops

    • Size. Each Zürich through station has 4 tracks. Paris Nord-Est would have 24 to 26, of which 16 to 20 for high-speed trains. Zürich is no evidence for a station of that size.
    • The hall stayed. About two thirds of Zürich's long-distance trains still end or turn back in the hall (derived). The Paris project moves all main-line trains underground. Zürich shows that through platforms relieve a terminus, not that they can replace one.
    • Trains and length. The platforms compare: 420 m in Zürich, 400 m for a double high-speed train in Paris.18 The traffic does not: 140 long-distance trains a day use Löwenstrasse, about nine departures an hour. The pattern tested for Paris has 12 high-speed trains an hour running through each way and 6 more that reverse: see the hour.
    • Depth and price. Löwenstrasse lies 16 m down and was dug from above. In 2026 euros it cost €0.5 million to €0.6 million per metre of platform track, against the €1.0 million used for the deeper Paris stations: see the prices.
    • Stops. Running through did not shorten the stop of trains that wait for connections. A train that turns back in Zürich stands 5 to 12 minutes; this study takes 8 minutes for a train that reverses at Paris Nord-Est: see reversing.
    • Time. Nine years from vote to opening for the first station, and fourteen for the second, from the vote of 2001 to the long-distance trains of December 2015.
    The reading

    Zürich supports three claims of this study: through tracks under a terminus add much capacity for their number, they can be built while the station works, and voters will pay for them when the alternative is a worse station further away. It does not support the size, the depth or the cost of the Paris stations, and its long-distance trains gained less time at the platform than one might expect.

    Annex B

    The Elizabeth line: joining two sides of a capital

    London's Elizabeth line is the closest recent case of joining two sides of a capital by a deep tunnel with large stations. It opened in 2022, three and a half years late and 28% over budget. It now carries more than 700,000 trips a day and its fares cover its running cost, yet most of its passengers were already on rail and save a few minutes each. It is also far smaller and simpler than what Paris would need.

    The line and its stations

    Stopping trains from the west used to end at Paddington station, and stopping trains from the east at Liverpool Street station, two terminals at the edge of the centre.208 The project, called Crossrail while it was built, joined them with 21 km of new twin tunnel under central London, one tube for each direction, and added a branch to the south-east.209 The result is one line of more than 100 km and 41 stations, 10 of them new.210 It is run by Transport for London (TfL), the city's transport authority.

    205mtrains, all alikeEach for up to 1,500 people213 214

    Each mined station has two platform tunnels of about 240 m, and most have a ticket hall at each end, so that one station spans two older ones.216 217 The underground stations have platform screen doors, glass walls between the platform and the track.218 All 41 stations can be used without steps.212

    Journey times before and after

    Paddington to Liverpool Street takes 11 minutes instead of about 20.215 The largest gains are on the new south-east branch, which had no direct railway to the centre. On the older branches the saving is smaller, but the change of train at the terminal disappears. Where the Underground already ran directly, the line saves nothing.

    What the official evaluation measured

    TfL and the national transport ministry published an evaluation of the first two years in 2025.214 It counts perceived minutes: minutes weighted for waiting, crowding and delay, as a passenger feels them.

    A weekday of October 2023TripsMinutes saved per tripMinutes saved in all
    New public transport trips71,0006.3447,000
    Trips already made, anywhere in London6,429,0001.38,552,000
    All trips6,500,0001.48,999,000
    • Small savings for many people. 95% of the minutes saved go to trips that were already being made (derived), including on other lines that became less crowded.
    • Measured from door to door, the typical peak journey between the Paddington area and the Abbey Wood area fell from 74.5 to 45 minutes between 2019 and 2023.214
    • Along the older branches many routes show no significant fall, since trains already ran there. The report gives no minutes for the change of train that disappeared.214

    How traffic grew, and where it came from

    The line opened in three steps over twelve months, and traffic rose at each one. Against the last year before the pandemic, yearly journeys have multiplied by 4.3: from 56 million on the two older services to 242 million in 2025/26 (derived).104 105

    Where the passengers came from

    • New trips are about a tenth. The evaluation finds 71,000 more public transport trips a weekday across London, about 1% of the city's total and a tenth of the line's own (derived).214 TfL's first estimate, a year after opening, was twice that (unverified).251
    • The older services kept their traffic; the growth is elsewhere. The traffic that came from them equals about 58 million journeys a year, almost what they carried in 2019/20 (derived).250 104
    • Other lines were relieved. Parallel rail links carry 16% to 22% less than comparable links (derived).214 The line itself has room: in January 2024 it was never above 3 standing passengers per square metre.214
    What this says for a forecast

    Most users of a new through line are people already on rail who save a few minutes. New trips are about a tenth, and the shift from cars is close to nothing. Demand rose 6% to 9% where journeys became 10% shorter.250 This study builds its regional forecast the same way, with an average saving of 2.3 minutes a journey: see regional traffic and the evidence.

    What it cost, who paid, and what came back

    £18.9bnfinal costBudget of 2010: £14.8 billion. Trains and depot, £1.1 billion, come on top65
    3½yearslatePlanned for December 2018, opened in May 202265
    37%paid through London's government£6.9 billion of the £18.8 billion of final funding, raised on business property and developers (derived)252 65
    £177mfares above running costIn 2025/26 (derived)105

    In 2026 euros the final cost is about €32 billion, an order of magnitude converted for this study with British consumer prices and the exchange rate of October 2026.65 253 254 The tunnels were finished in 2015.56 The time was lost afterwards, in the stations and in making trains, signalling and station equipment work together; the delay became apparent only in late 2018.255 Of the last £1.9 billion of cost increase, £0.9 billion was the cost of the delay itself.256

    Who paid

    The supplement on business rates. Business rates are the British tax on business property, charged on the rental value of the premises. Since 2010 London adds 2 pence per pound of that value, the legal maximum, on its larger premises, 13% of them.252 The supplement was to pay £4.1 billion, 28% of the budget of 2010 (derived).233

    The overrun was covered by government loans, most of them to the Greater London Authority, the city's government.256 With a levy on new floorspace paid by developers, the Authority's contribution reached £6.9 billion, 37% of the final funding of £18.8 billion (derived).252 65 It borrowed the money and repays it from the two levies. The supplement is due to end between 2038 and 2041.252

    Year to March, £ millionSupplement collectedInterestDebt repaidDebt left
    2023142235150not published4,500
    2025257 2582481252543,800

    Rounded figures. The Authority borrowed £3.3 billion, then £2.1 billion from the government.142 252 In the year to March 2027 the loan costs about £361 million against £290 million from the supplement; the rest comes from the levy on developers or from reserves (derived). £290 million is about €340 million.253

    Fares and running cost

    The line earns more in fares than it costs to run: £177 million more in 2025/26 (derived).105 Two cautions. The surplus is about half of what the Authority pays each year on its loan, and the two sit in different accounts. And at most about half of the income is new to TfL: the rest was already paid on its other lines (derived).250

    For Paris the picture is different. In the central case of this study the new income covers 56% of the yearly running cost: see the operations account. How London's supplement serves as a precedent is in the financing precedents.

    Benefits against costs

    A benefit to cost ratio divides what a project is expected to bring, counted in money over 60 years, by what it costs. Above 1, it gives back more than it costs. "Wider benefits" are gains beyond time saved, mainly the extra output of firms and workers brought closer together; they are harder to estimate.

    What the official evaluation does not show
    • No value for money yet. "It is still too early for an in-depth analysis of the Elizabeth line's value for money."214
    • No result on property or tax. No measured effect on property values or on tax receipts has been published. The figures in circulation, such as "£42 billion added to the economy", are forecasts made by the promoter before the opening.157 156 261
    • Homes and jobs without a cause. 71,000 homes were built within 1 km of stations from 2015 to 2024, and jobs grew, mostly in the City, where the report cannot tell the line's effect apart.106

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What Paris can take from it

    • The risk is in the stations and the systems, not in the tunnels. Main station contracts tripled or more: Paddington from £181 million to £571 million.80
    • Do not fix the opening date early. The project was "dominated by a fixed completion date" set eight years ahead.255 The official lesson: "Use an evidenced range rather than a single target date."263
    • Fewer contracts, and one body in charge of the joins. With 36 main contracts and nobody but the client managing the joins between them, the client paid for knock-on delays.80
    • Protect the testing period. Trains switch between three signalling systems.80 Preparing the line for service took 14 months against 4 assumed.240
    • Open in stages, and plan the stages again when delay comes.240 For Paris see the stages.
    • Price the stations with care. London's central stations cost €2.0 million per metre of platform track, twice the €1.0 million used here. At the London price layout A would cost about €32 billion more: see the prices used.

    Where the comparison stops

    • London built a large metro. One kind of train, 205 m long. Its 24 trains an hour need only two platform tracks per station. No long-distance train uses the tunnel.
    • Paris would take 400 m high-speed trains. They stand longer at the platform than a metro, so Paris Nord-Est needs 24 to 26 tracks: see how many platforms. Nobody has built a deep station of that size.
    • London joined two suburban networks. Paris would also join four high-speed lines.
    • The cost is of another order: €70 billion for layout A against about €32 billion.
    • London's fares pay for running the line. In this study the new income covers 56% of the running cost.
    • A planned frequency is not a promise. The line runs 16 trains an hour at quieter times where its sponsors required 20.243
    The reading

    The Elizabeth line shows that a through tunnel under a capital fills up fast, relieves the lines beside it and can pay for its own running. It also shows that most of the traffic is moved from other lines, and that stations and systems decide cost and delay. Its evaluators warn against carrying the results to other places.214 Zürich, the other precedent, is closer to Paris in kind, with long-distance trains under a working terminal: see Zürich main station.

    Annex C

    The Swiss pulse: every train meets every train

    In Switzerland the timetable was designed first and the works second. Trains from every direction reach the main stations just before the hour and leave just after, so that almost any change takes a few minutes. Lines were made faster only as far as needed to run from one such meeting to the next in under an hour.

    The idea: all the trains are in the station together

    A regular-interval timetable repeats itself every hour: each line leaves at the same minutes all day. The Swiss network has had one since 23 May 1982.264 The pulse adds a second rule. At the main stations, called nodes, the trains of all lines arrive at about the same time and leave again together a few minutes later.265 In the words of SBB, the Swiss federal railway, trains and buses reach a node just before the full and the half hour, or at minutes 15 and 45, and leave shortly after.266 The passenger does not hunt for a connection: it is standing at another platform.

    :45

    Arrivals

      Departures

        Minute, line, place and track for the wave around the full hour. Tracks 31 to 34 are the through platforms under the hall.

        The station's standard minimum for a change is 7 minutes.176 Shorter changes exist where the planner names the pair of trains: Bern to St. Gallen is sold with 4 minutes, because the two trains stand on the two sides of one platform.206 Where no value is set, Swiss timetable data assume 2 minutes.267

        The nodes and the minute at which they beat

        The plan of 1994 named seven nodes. Zürich, Basel, Bern and Winterthur are served at the full hour and, for a large part, at the half hour. Lausanne, Biel and Luzern are served at minutes 15 and 45, because the runs to them are slightly too long for the hour. A node at 15 and 45 needs a train every half hour to give good connections.265

        The 2026 timetable still shows Zürich, Bern and Basel at 00 and 30, and Lausanne and Biel at 15 and 45. Luzern now gathers its trains around the hour, and St. Gallen behaves as a node of its own (derived from the timetable). Choose a station or a line.

        The plan is the Federal Council's.265 The 2026 columns are derived from the timetable. Passengers per working day in 2023, shown in the panel, are SBB counts.201 Zürich is described by its canton as by far the largest interchange node of the network.283

        Why a run must take just under an hour

        If every train is in Zürich at the hour and every train is in Bern at the hour, a train between the two has just under an hour for the run. The Federal Council put it in one sentence: the concept requires journey times between the nodes of a little under one hour.265 In general the run, with half the stop at each end, must fit a multiple of half the interval: 30, 60 or 90 minutes for an hourly service (unverified).284 Hence the Swiss motto of 1986: not as fast as technically possible, but as quickly as necessary.268

        The same thing on the real board. In 2026 the train from Zürich reaches Bern at :58. The trains to Basel and to Lausanne and Geneva leave at :04, the train to Visp and Brig at :07.285 270 With the 69 minutes of before 2004, it would arrive at :11, after all of them (illustration).

        Where the hour cannot be reached, the node moves. Bern to Lausanne takes 69 minutes, so Lausanne is a node at 15 and 45: the train leaves Bern at :34 and arrives at :43.288 265 Official maps show slots of 60 and 75 minutes on these western lines.289 A target of 57 minutes exists but has not been met,290 and the plan for 2035 assumes 68.291 The western cantons speak of a two-tier network.292

        What it took

        • A vote. On 6 December 1987, 57.0% of voters approved Rail 2000, on a turnout of 47.7%.293
        • A budget that was cut to fit. The credit was CHF 5.4 billion at 1985 prices, about CHF 7.4 billion at 1993 prices. By 1991 the railway's plans would have cost about CHF 16 billion. The first stage was then capped at CHF 7.4 billion.265 Of four new lines in the plan put to voters, one was kept.294
        • One new line. Between Mattstetten and Rothrist, on the way from Bern to Olten: 45 km (47 km in two official papers), for CHF 1.5 billion in the press of 2002 and CHF 1,458 million in the budget of 1994.286 295 266 265 It brought three runs to about one hour at once: Zürich to Bern, Bern to Basel and Bern to Luzern.
        • Trains instead of concrete elsewhere. On the line along the Jura from Lausanne to Zürich through Biel, tilting trains were bought instead of new line. Double-deck coaches gave 40% more seats without longer platforms.265 Works were done only at bottlenecks or where a run between nodes took more than 60 minutes.296
        • The outturn. The first stage opened on 12 December 2004 and cost CHF 5.9 billion, CHF 1.5 billion under its ceiling.295 286

        Three runs came to about one hour with the new line. Three others, in the west, are still 8 to 11 minutes over the hour, and all three are slower than planned in 1994.

        What it gave

        93.2%of trains less than 3 minutes late2024; 94.1% in 2025201 304
        98.7%of connections made2022 to 2024201

        • The timetable of 2004. 12% more trains and 14% more train-km; about 90% of all times changed.307 Average long-distance journeys became 7% shorter and frequency rose by 20%.308 SBB carried 253.4 million passengers in 2004 and 275.9 million in 2005.309
        • How much is due to the pulse? The official evaluation credits slightly under half of the growth of 1996 to 2005 to the change in service. It judges the coordination of long-distance and regional trains at the nodes a success, but it could not separate the effect of the pulse from that of speed and frequency.305
        • The first step brought nothing at once. The regular-interval timetable of 1982 produced no measurable rise in traffic in its first year.310
        • Protecting it has a price. Since the end of 2024 a badly delayed train is held until the next slot of its pattern, half an hour later, rather than disturb the node.304 For 2025 journey times in western Switzerland were lengthened to keep trains on time and connections safe during works.311
        • A node is greedy in platforms. A station where all trains meet needs more platform tracks than any other pattern.312

        What it would mean for Paris

        An illustration, not a timetable

        This study has not drawn up a timetable. What follows shows what a pulse needs and what the through stations would make possible. No benefit of a pulse is counted in the model behind this report.

        A pulse needs one thing that Paris lacks: a place where the trains of all lines stand together. Today its main lines end in separate terminals, and a passenger between the north or east of France and the south-east or the Atlantic coast changes stations across the city. In the model this takes 57.5 minutes from train to train. At Paris Nord-Est, trains from the north and the east would stand in the same station as trains to the south-east and the Atlantic coast. A change there is taken as 12.5 minutes assumption, and about 47% of these passengers would not change at all, because a train runs through: see crossing Paris.

        A pulse costs platforms. The number of platforms in this report assumes that stops are spread through the hour: see how many platforms. A timetable in which trains meet at fixed minutes would need more tracks, for two reasons. More trains stand in the station at the same moment, and each stands longer: in Zürich a through train that waits for connections stops for 6 to 9 minutes, against 3 minutes for one that does not wait (derived, see Zürich).

        What a pulse at Paris Nord-Est would ask for

        • The same minutes every hour. The pattern tested in this report has 12 high-speed trains an hour each way running through: see the hour. A pulse would fix the minutes at which they meet.
        • Trains from the north and east in just before, trains to the south out just after, and the reverse half an hour later.
        • Platforms known in advance. In Switzerland a line uses the same track hour after hour, and the track is printed weeks ahead (derived).270 Platforms show where each coach stops.45
        • Trains on time. The Swiss pulse rests on more than nine trains in ten arriving within three minutes.201

        Where the Swiss example stops

        • The French timetable is not built this way. High-speed trains do not leave at the same minutes every hour on every line (unverified).
        • Seats are reserved. A Swiss passenger who misses a connection takes the next train half an hour later. A reserved seat is for one train, so a missed connection costs more and the margin must be wider. Today the platform is shown about 20 minutes before departure and access closes 2 minutes before.43
        • Distances are longer. Swiss nodes are about an hour apart, so every train meets a node every hour. On French high-speed lines only Paris itself would be such a meeting point.
        • Few passengers change. In German long-distance travel 18% of trips include a change between long-distance trains.313 In this study about 5.2 million journeys a year change between Paris stations.
        • A pulse fills the platforms at the same minute. A station where all trains meet needs the most tracks of any pattern.312 The stations of this report are not sized for it.
        The reading

        The through stations are not a pulse, and this report does not need one. They remove what makes a pulse impossible in Paris today: separate stations. Whether French high-speed trains should then meet at fixed minutes is a choice of timetable that can be made later. It would need regular trains that run on time, and perhaps more platforms.

        Annex D

        How the numbers are made

        Enough detail to check the figures or to redo them with better data. Everything is computed by a small open model: Python scripts whose results feed every number in this document, and the same arithmetic in the browser for the calculators.

        The access model

        • Points: 1,000 points on an even grid over Paris, 315 m apart. For the suburbs, the centre of each of 1,265 communes, weighted by population.
        • Network: every metro, RER and tram line, and the suburban train lines for the communes outside Paris, with stations, stop order and published interchange times, from the data of Île-de-France Mobilités of 5 October 2026.71 Buses are not included.
        • Speeds: walking at 4.5 km/h on a path 30% longer than the straight line; each metro line at its own average speed (20 to 28.5 km/h); RER at 60 km/h plus one minute per stop. Waiting is half the interval between trains. In the suburbs, up to 1 km on foot to a station, further at 20 km/h.
        • Result: the quickest time from each point to the hall of each of the four terminals, and to the Nord-Est station taken as the nearer of its two halls.
        • Two stops: for each direction the passenger boards at the home station of the train or at its other Paris stop. Two measures are kept. The plain one is the time to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops; it is the one shown first on the map. The stricter one adds the minutes the train then takes between its two stops (10 minutes from Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and 11 to Montparnasse, stop included assumption); it is the one used to count benefits.
        • Never longer than today: each train still stops where it does now, so no point can lose on either measure. The export script stops with an error if one does.
        • Time inside the station is not in these figures. It is compared separately (see inside the station) and tested as two extra minutes for everyone (see the tests).
        • Weights: one run on the clock; one with the official weights on walking, waiting and changing; one with metro and RER riding counted 25% heavier for crowding.

        New passengers are valued at half the time saved, as in every transport appraisal: they gain less than those who already travelled. Yearly figures mix sources that turn a weekday count into a year with factors from 273 to 435, and base years from 2012 to 2025; they are orders of magnitude, not counts.

        Official rules that are not applied. A full French appraisal would let the value of time rise with income, discount at 3.2% to 4.6% instead of 3%,316 and count each euro of public money as 1.2 euros.72 The first helps the project and the other two count against it. The central case applies none of them; growth of benefits and the two discount rates are tested in the tests, and growth is used for the comparison with other projects in the economic return.

        Cost

        Quantities times unit prices from built projects, plus 20% for design and client costs, 7% for land and 30% for risk; the prices, their sources and the test against seven projects are in the cost chapter. Stations are sized by one rule: 5 stops an hour per platform track, a reversing train counted as 2.25 stops, for the southern lines at their planned capacity (see platforms).

        The two accounts, the return and taxes

        • Yearly repayment. Construction cost, increased by interest during 12 years of even spending, repaid in equal yearly amounts over 60 years at 3% above inflation: each €1 billion costs €43 million a year.
        • Operations account. Costs: running the stations at the rate recorded on the first RER E section (€13,200 a year per metre of platform track) and the tunnels at €2.25 million per km, midway between that record (€3.5 million) and the average of the RER network (€1.0 million); one renewal of the tunnels' rail systems after 30 years, set aside evenly; extra running of regional trains. What today's terminals cost to run is not deducted. Income: the charge, track charges on the net change in high-speed journeys, new Navigo passes, regional express fares, the authority's fee, shop rents.
        • The charge. Journeys fall by the fare response: a charge of c on a fare of €48.50 keeps (1 + c / fare) to the power -0.7 of the journeys.118 The fare is the average revenue per journey before VAT, and the same fare is used for passengers who cross Paris; both overstate the loss. A response of -0.5 is shown beside the central one. Track charges are taken to follow the net change in journeys assumption. No VAT is counted on the charge.
        • Navigo. New suburban journeys, times the share made by new pass holders, divided by 420 journeys a year per commuter, times the price of a yearly pass.
        • Capital account. The yearly repayment plus any shortfall of operations, less land sales, a tax on businesses of the size of the Grand Paris Express one and a European grant; what is left is expressed as a grant paid during the works.
        • Economic return. Yearly benefits divided by yearly cost. Benefits are the time saved, comfort and wider effects, less the value of the journeys given up because of the charge. The ticket money of train operators is not counted. With benefits growing g a year, the level yearly amount of the same value over 60 years is used; passenger numbers, and so the charge and the shops, grow at 60% of g, and running costs stay flat assumption. The rate of return is the discount rate at which 60 years of benefits less running costs equal the construction cost.
        • What public budgets get back. VAT at 10% inside the net change in ticket money, less fuel duty on car trips moved to rail. Then three readings of the added activity: none of it is new for the country; or it is counted as in the appraisal the ratios come from (each job worth €10,000 a year of benefits saved, output from denser job markets and from working time saved on the clock taxed at 43.6%); or every job implied is new and taxed on the average output of a job in the region.

        The scripts are in the model folder of the repository: nordest.py (access, traffic, cost), finance.py (accounts, return, taxes), export.py (data for this site). src/js/model.js repeats the accounts in the browser and is checked against the Python results to fifteen digits.

        What has been checked, and what has not

        • Checked twice by an independent reviewer: the access model, the traffic estimates and the construction cost, for an earlier report.
        • Checked once, on 12 October 2026, and corrected: the two accounts, the passenger charge, the Navigo estimate, what public budgets get back and the comparison with other projects. The reviewer's main corrections were to the running cost of tunnels, now set between two French records where the first version used the higher one; to the tax estimate, now given as three readings; and to the comparison with other projects, whose bases differ. The corrected version has not been checked again.
        • Not checked against outside sources by anyone but their authors: the three annexes on Zürich, the Elizabeth line and the Swiss timetable, and the drawings of stations and works, which are sketches.
        • Access times are times to the entrance of a station. No minutes are added for the depth of platforms; time inside the station is treated separately.
